turns.t: Right, Sam, the booking note says you've swallowed a bit of Lego. Is that right?
Um... yeah. I swallowed a bit of Lego. A little one. A flat grey piece.
Okay. Tell me what happened, from the start.
I was... um... holding it in my mouth. While I was building a spaceship. And then I sort of... gulped.
Ah, that happens more than you'd think. When was this?
Yesterday. After tea. Or... no, it was before tea, actually.
Yesterday, before tea. Did it go down easily, or did it get stuck anywhere?
It just went down. Straight away. It was a bit... um, weird.
Any trouble breathing once it had gone down?
No. It was fine.
Any being sick or vomiting afterwards?
No... um, no. I wasn't sick.
Good. And how is your tummy feeling now?
It's... a bit achy. Not horrible. Just a tummy ache.
Would you call it mild, moderate or severe?
Mild. I think. Um... yeah, mild.
When did the ache start?
This morning.
Can you point to where it is for me?
Here. Um. Round my belly button, like.
Does anything make it better or worse? Think about eating, or moving around.
Um... it's a bit worse when I run around. And lying down helps.
Sensible. Now let's check your regular medicines. Do you take anything every day?
Yes. A puffer, I think. And... something for my... um...
Take your time. What's the puffer for?
For my asthma. The blue one. Salbutamol.
Good. How much of it, and how often do you use it?
Um... 100 micrograms. When I need it. Mum says it's written on the side.
That's right, I can see that on your record. What else is there?
A cream, for my eczema. Hydrocortisone. Once a day, on my elbows.
And the last one?
Um... Movicol. The sachets. For my constipation. Mum makes me have it in orange juice. One sachet a day.
That one's useful today. Keeping it going helps things move along.
Will it help the Lego come out?
It'll certainly not hurt. Hop up on the couch, and I'll have a feel of your tummy.
Is it going to be cold? Last time the doctor's hands were freezing.
I've warmed them up, promise. Tell me if anything hurts when I press.
Your tummy is soft, which is what I wanted to feel. You can sit up again.
So what's going to happen to the Lego?
Here's what I think. It's small, smooth plastic, so most likely it will pass through on its own.
When?
Usually within a few days. It comes out with your poo, and you won't feel a thing.
Do I have to look in the toilet for it? That's gross.
A quick look each day, please, with mum or dad helping. Just so we know it has gone.
Um. Okay. I'll make my brother do it.
Ha, nice try. Now, here's what you can do while you wait. Eat normally, with lots of fruit and veg.
And chips?
Sometimes. Drink plenty of water too, and keep taking your Movicol every day.
Okay. Can I still build stuff?
Yes, but not in your mouth. Lego goes in the box and nowhere else.
Ha. Okay. Um, I won't.
If the ache gets bad, or you're sick, or you feel hot and unwell, tell mum and come straight in.
Okay. I'll tell her. She'll probably tell me anyway.
I'd like to see you again in three days, to check how things are going.
Um, can it be after school?
I'll ask reception to find you an afternoon slot. Off you go, Sam, and well done for being so brave.
Thanks, doctor. Bye.

clinical_assessment.assessment: most likely it will pass through on its own
clinical_assessment.normalized_assessment: Swallowed small plastic piece likely to pass spontaneously

clinical_actions.description: Check stool daily for the Lego piece
Eat normally with fruit and vegetables, drink plenty of water and keep taking Movicol daily
Return promptly if abdominal pain worsens, vomiting or feeling hot and unwell
